      "startEvent": 1876,
      "endEvent": 1886,
      "contextStartEvent": 1846,
      "contextEndEvent": 1941,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "So if naturalism were true, we could never know that evolution is unguided",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": [
        "none"
      ],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Craig disallows observations of reliable cognition as a naturalist rebuttal, then treats actual reliability as evidence against naturalism (E1876–1886). This could protect the probability premise from contrary findings. However, E1860–1875 supplies an explicit argument about cognitive reliability; whether its evidential restriction is independently warranted remains disputed, with A replying at E1920–1941."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2172,
      "endEvent": 2184,
      "contextStartEvent": 2166,
      "contextEndEvent": 2190,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "our faculties are probably not reliable regardless of appearances",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": [
        "none"
      ],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "After A's intervening empirical analogy (E1920–1941), Craig renews the restriction that apparent reliability cannot answer the evolutionary objection and attributes dismissal to failure to grasp it (E2172–2184). Yet he supplies the selection-versus-truth rationale again. The passage may shield that premise, but does not clearly reject objections regardless of their merits."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2386,
      "endEvent": 2390,
      "contextStartEvent": 2380,
      "contextEndEvent": 2412,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "any argument against that is going to be less plausible than that claim itself",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "yes",
      "emotionalDevices": [
        "none"
      ],
      "confidence": "high",
      "explanation": "Wielenberg explicitly ranks every argument against objective moral facts below the belief itself (E2386–2390), protecting that commitment in advance without examining individual objections. This is an epistemic policy, not a compact slogan replacing an argument. He describes a shared debate starting point; his attribution of this policy to Craig is not independent evidence of Craig endorsing it."
    }
  ],
  "contrasts": [
    {
      "startEvent": 2436,
      "endEvent": 2474,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "That obviously knocks down if my arguments succeed just one competitor to my view.",
      "explanation": "The Churchill catchphrase introduces a qualified comparison. Wielenberg explicitly acknowledges that defeating Craig's account would eliminate only one alternative and that a full argument requires much more."
    },

      "startEvent": 2475,
      "endEvent": 2493,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "Which one has the balance of evidence and argument in its favor?",
      "explanation": "Craig explains why comparative plausibility, rather than certainty, is the relevant standard for both speakers. His concluding metaphor about certainty summarizes that methodological distinction rather than replacing its explanation."
    }
